h.select_rule: Keep hypotheses whose signed direction follows almost mechanically from the edited field's own current value or from disconnection of the edited part, given the edit's usual sign. Drop those with an uncertain usual sign or with competing effects. Use any single condition at most three times.
h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to rank settings as strong, weak, neutral or harmful, and to note which settings cut off other parts from the outcome. Propose many candidates of two reliable kinds: self-conditioning, where removing or downgrading a strong current value is more negative than doing so to a weak one, and filling an empty or harmful slot is more positive; and disconnection, where an edit cut off from the outcome has an effect near zero, so its effect is lower than usual if it normally helps and higher if it normally hurts. Directions always refer to the signed effect. Spread hypotheses across different edit fields, values and conditions so that no single wrong assumption sinks many of them. Give a one-sentence mechanism and the edit's usual sign.

hyps.why: Removing an edge normally hurts, but it is harmless when node 1 is dead.
Dropping edge 4 usually hurts, but it is already disconnected when edge 0 is none.
Node 1 is dead when edge 0 is none, so a conv on edge 4 contributes nothing.
Removing edge 1 normally hurts, but it is harmless when node 2 has no path to the output.
Removing edge 2 is free when node 2 is cut off from the output.
Node 2 reaches the output only through edge 5, so with edge 5 none a conv on edge 1 is cut off.
Removing a strong conv hurts more than removing a weak or absent operation.
Deleting a strong first-layer conv costs more than deleting a weak one.
Losing a strong conv into the output hurts more than losing a weak edge.
Deleting a strong conv hurts more than deleting a weak or absent one.
